title: Telling people there's an AI behind it
promise: You'll know when you have to say there's an AI behind something, how to say it without it reading like small print, and what you answer when someone asks you to your face. By the end you'll have your notices written and one of them tested on a real person.
why: Álvaro set up an assistant to answer his patients' questions on WhatsApp outside opening hours. It worked well. A patient wrote asking whether she could come to her session with a recent injury, the assistant gave her a reasonable answer, and she came. In the consultation she said: «you told me so on WhatsApp». He hadn't told her anything. She had no way of knowing, and it wasn't a small detail: she had made a decision about her health believing she was talking to her physiotherapist.

theory.title: The rule isn't legal, it's about trust
theory.text: Before looking at what the regulations require, there's a question that gets it right nearly every time: is this person making a different decision because they believe a human is answering? If the answer is yes, you have to tell them. It isn't a compliance matter, it's about the other person being able to weigh what reaches them. A text from a professional carries one weight; one from a machine carries another. Taking that information away from someone takes away their ability to decide well, and that gets noticed late and lands badly. And there's a practical point too: most people don't get annoyed that you use AI, they get annoyed that you didn't tell them.
theory.analogy: It's the «previously frozen» note on a menu. Almost nobody minds; everybody minds finding out afterwards.
theory.example: Álvaro's patient wasn't upset about the assistant. She was upset about having decided to come with an injury believing he had told her to.

theory.title: The three cases where you always disclose
theory.text: First: when someone might believe they're talking to a person. A chat, a WhatsApp assistant, an automatic reply to an email. There the notice goes at the start of the conversation, not at the end. Second: when what the AI produces is used to decide something affecting somebody. A summary of a job application, an assessment, a triage. There you have to say which part the machine did and which part a person reviewed. And third: when the content you publish is generated, and especially if it's an image, a voice or a video that looks real. In that third case the notice isn't courtesy: it's what separates an illustration from a deception.
theory.example: Álvaro's case is the first. An automatic report deciding who gets called first is the second. A generated photo of premises that don't exist is the third.

theory.title: How to disclose without it reading like small print
theory.text: A notice works if it's read, and it's read if it's where people look and written the way people talk. «This service utilises artificial intelligence systems» is read by nobody. «You're talking to an automatic assistant. If you need to speak to me, type HUMAN and I'll call you» is read by everybody, because it also tells them what to do. That's the point: a good notice doesn't only inform, it offers the way out. And it goes at the start, in the first message, not in a footer or behind a link to terms.
theory.example: First message from Álvaro's assistant: «Hello, I'm the clinic's automatic assistant. I can give you opening hours, prices and general advice. For anything about your injury, type CONSULT and Álvaro will answer in person.»

theory.title: The way out to a human isn't optional
theory.text: Any setup that talks to people has to have a clear escape door to you, and it has to work. It's the part most often neglected and the one that prevents the most trouble, because the moment someone needs it is usually the moment something important is at stake. And there's a second half people forget: it isn't enough that the person can ask for it, you have to find out. If the keyword doesn't reach you as a notification somewhere you actually look, the door is painted on the wall.
theory.example: Álvaro set CONSULT to send him a message on his phone. He gets two or three a week and they're exactly the conversations his assistant had no business being in.

theory.title: Limits have to be stated, not hidden
theory.text: Saying what your setup isn't for protects the other person and protects you. «I can't give medical advice», «I can't confirm prices for special orders», «I can't change your appointment, call for that». Writing it into the opening notice does two things at once: it stops someone using it for something it shouldn't do, and it saves you having to answer for advice you didn't give. And it's useful information, not a disclaimer: whoever reads it knows what they can ask for and what they can't.
theory.example: «I can give you opening hours, prices and general exercises. I can't assess an injury or tell you whether you should come in: Álvaro looks at that.» Notice the second sentence isn't a liability waiver: it's useful information. Whoever reads it knows exactly what to ask the assistant and what to save for the consultation, and stops trying things that were going to go badly.

theory.title: What you answer when they ask you
theory.text: They will ask, and it's worth having the answer ready because improvising here goes badly. The one that works has three parts and it's short: what you use it for, what you review yourself, and what you don't leave to the machine. Said that way, without getting defensive, the conversation ends there and it ends well. What goes badly is the opposite: minimising it («it's just a little helper») or launching into an explanation of how the technology works. Nobody is asking that: they're asking what they can rely on.
theory.example: «I use an assistant for questions about opening hours and prices outside consultation time. Anything to do with your treatment I answer myself, and the assistant passes you to me as soon as that comes up.»

tasks.title: Check whether any of your setups talks to people
tasks.action: Go back over what you've built and mark which ones meet any of the three cases: someone might believe they're talking to you, what comes out is used to decide something about someone, or it publishes generated content. If none applies, this lesson still serves you for the final project and you can do the tasks on a hypothetical.
tasks.expect: A short list, perhaps of one. The commonest is the first case, with a form that replies automatically or a messaging assistant.
tasks.stuck: Watch out for automatic email replies drafted by AI: they count as the first case even though they aren't a chat, because they go out under your name.

tasks.title: Write your opening notice
tasks.where: In a file, then in the setup
tasks.action: Write your assistant's first message with four things and in this order: that it's automatic, what it's for, what it isn't for, and how to reach you. Four lines at most and written the way you talk, not the way a contract does.
tasks.prompt:
Hello, I'm the automatic assistant for [YOUR BUSINESS].
I can help you with: [THE THREE THINGS IT DOES].
I can't help with: [WHAT IT SHOULDN'T TOUCH].
To talk to [YOUR NAME], type [WORD] and they'll answer in person.
tasks.expect: Four lines. Read them aloud: if they sound like terms and conditions, rewrite them the way you'd say it to a client at the counter.
tasks.stuck: If you're struggling to decide the «I can't», look at the three or four topics where a wrong answer would genuinely land you in trouble. Those are the ones.

tasks.title: Build the way out to a human and check it reaches you
tasks.action: Two things. That the keyword stops the assistant and it doesn't keep answering, and that it sends you a notification wherever you actually look: phone, email or whichever channel you use. Then test it yourself by typing the word from another phone or another account.
tasks.expect: The assistant goes quiet and the notification reaches you. If the assistant carries on answering after the keyword, the door doesn't work: that's worse than not having one, because the person believes they've already called you.
tasks.stuck: If you can't get it to stop, the simplest version works: have the keyword make the workflow send one fixed message («[name] has been notified, they'll get back to you as soon as they can») and not reply again in that conversation for 24 hours.

tasks.title: Have the AI find the holes in your notice
tasks.action: Give it your notice and your business context, and ask it to think like the user, not like a lawyer.
tasks.prompt:
I have an automatic assistant that talks to [MY CLIENTS / PATIENTS / STUDENTS] on [CHANNEL: WhatsApp, web, email]. I work in [SECTOR].

MY OPENING NOTICE:
[PASTE YOUR TEXT]

Put yourself in the position of the person reading it, not of a lawyer:
1. What could they misunderstand or take for granted after reading this?
2. What topic might they ask the assistant about believing I'm the one answering, and that would be a serious problem in my sector? Give me three concrete examples, with the sentence that person would type.
3. Does the notice make clear how to reach me? If not, how would you rewrite it, in one line?

Don't give me legal text or terms of use. Only what can be misunderstood.
tasks.expect: Two or three situations you hadn't thought of, with the literal sentence someone would type. Those sentences are perfect for testing your setup.
tasks.stuck: If it hands you a long legal text, say: «Not that. Give me three exact sentences a client of mine would type that my assistant shouldn't answer.»

tasks.title: Test it on a real person
tasks.action: Ask someone who doesn't know the setup to talk to your assistant for five minutes, without explaining anything beforehand. Then ask them three questions: whether it was clear from the start that it was automatic, whether they knew how to reach you, and whether at any point they thought you were the one answering.
tasks.expect: Three honest answers. If on the third they say they weren't sure, you have work to do: the notice isn't working even though it's written.
tasks.stuck: If you have nobody to ask, leave it a week and reread the conversation from the start yourself as though you knew nothing. It isn't as good as a real person, but it catches the big things.

tasks.title: Write your three-part answer
tasks.action: Write, in three sentences, what you'll say when someone asks whether you use AI: what you use it for, what you review yourself, and what you don't leave to it. Learn it roughly by heart, because you'll be saying it out loud and it doesn't improvise well in the moment.
tasks.expect: Three sentences. Keep them next to the data and tools file from lesson 41: the two get asked about at the same time and it helps to have them together.
tasks.stuck: If while writing the third part nothing comes to mind that you don't leave to the machine, stop: that probably means there's something you should be reviewing and aren't.

matters: That the question is whether someone would decide differently knowing a machine is answering.
That the notice goes at the start and in people's language, not in a footer.
That the way out to a human has to work and you have to find out about it.
That almost nobody minds you using AI: they mind not having known.
ignore: Drafting long terms of use. Four lines that get read are worth more than two pages that don't.
The debates about whether everything should be labelled. Start with the three clear cases.
Putting the notice in the footer. Nobody reads it there and it doesn't count.
canDo: Know which of the three cases you're in and whether you have to disclose.
Write a notice that gets read and that offers the way out.
Build a handover to a human that works and that you find out about.
Answer in three sentences when someone asks whether you use AI.
cantDo: Stop someone using your assistant for something it shouldn't do: only reduce it and hand over.
Replace legal advice in regulated sectors.
Delegate responsibility to the machine: what goes out under your name is yours.
Know whether the notice works without testing it on a person.
words: Telling the person that what's answering them is an automatic system. It goes at the start.
The word or button that stops the assistant and notifies you. It has to genuinely work.
What you say your setup can't do. It protects the other person and it protects you.
Which part of what comes out is looked at by a person before it's delivered.
Text, image, voice or video made by AI. When it looks real, disclosing stops being courtesy.
next: You close the security block with the keys stored, the data sorted, the spending bounded and what needs saying said. Block 10, the last one, is about turning all this into something you can show, defend and charge for.
